question: What is the main reason we use stitches to close a simple skin cut?

options.A: To reduce healing time and minimize scarring
options.B: To stop deep muscle spasms near the injury site
options.C: To permanently eliminate all risk of bacterial infection
options.D: To replace the need for a tetanus toxoid booster

explanation: You've got this! Bringing the skin edges neatly together helps the cut heal much faster and keeps the scar as small as possible. Great job!

question: Why must you check when a patient had their last tetanus shot before stitching up a wound?

options.A: To determine if the patient needs protection against tetanus spores in dirty wounds
options.B: To check how fast the patient's blood will normally clot
options.C: To decide what type of local anesthetic to inject
options.D: To calculate the exact day the sutures should be removed

explanation: Cuts can easily trap dirt and tetanus bacteria. Checking their history helps us know if they need a booster shot to stay safe. Simple and lifesaving!

question: Which tool do nurses use to hold and guide a suture needle securely through the skin?
explanation: Spot on! A needle holder has special grip jaws built to hold a curved needle firmly so it doesn't slip or bend while you work.

question: Where should you NEVER inject a local painkiller (anesthetic) that contains adrenaline?

options.A: On the tip of the nose or fingers
options.B: Across the front of the thigh
options.C: On the fleshy part of the upper back

explanation: Adrenaline makes blood vessels squeeze shut. In delicate areas like fingers and noses, this can completely cut off blood supply and damage the tissue. Good to know for clinical practice!

question: What is the best way to wash loose dirt and germs out of a fresh cut?

options.A: Soaking the entire wound in a tub of tap water
options.B: Scrubbing the inside of the cut with dry gauze
options.D: Applying strong antiseptic solution directly into the tissue

explanation: Using a syringe with sterile saline creates just enough gentle pressure to wash away debris without harming the healing flesh. You're building great clinical skills!

question: Why should you avoid pouring harsh surgical scrubs directly inside an open wound?

options.A: It can damage exposed tissue cells and delay proper wound healing
options.B: It instantly inactivates any local anesthetic you inject later
options.C: It permanently stains the surrounding skin a bright yellow color
options.D: It causes the skin edges to swell up and prevent knot tying

explanation: Harsh chemicals are too strong for delicate exposed cells inside a wound. Stick to normal saline for cleaning—your patients will heal much better!

question: Which type of thread is used for outer skin stitches and needs to be taken out after a few days?
explanation: Non-absorbable materials like nylon give strong outer support while the skin heals, and we remove them during a follow-up visit. Easypz!

question: What is the big advantage of using a cutting needle when stitching tough skin?

options.A: Its sharp edge easily pierces through tough dermal layers
options.B: It stops the wound from bleeding during the procedure
options.C: It prevents the patient from feeling any sharp pain
options.D: It dissolves safely inside the body tissue after a week

explanation: Skin can be surprisingly tough! Cutting needles have a sharp edge designed to glide smoothly through without bending. You're mastering instrument basics.

question: At what angle should your needle enter the skin to create a smooth, curved stitch?
explanation: Entering at a 90-degree angle lets the curved needle follow its natural circular shape, making it glide right through the skin smoothly.

question: Where should your finished knot sit after tying a simple interrupted stitch?

options.A: Tucked tightly underneath the tissue forceps
options.B: Off to the side of the incision line
options.C: Buried deep underneath the subcutaneous fat layer
options.D: Directly in the center of the open wound gap

explanation: Always pull your knot off to the side! This keeps it from pressing down directly into the healing cut and causing irritation. Perfect technique!

question: Why do we usually remove facial stitches much sooner than stitches on the leg?

options.A: Facial skin heals slower and requires longer support
options.B: Facial sutures are always made of absorbable material
options.C: The face has a rich blood supply and skin marks easily
options.D: Legs experience much less daily movement than the face

explanation: The face gets loads of blood supply, so it heals super fast. Taking stitches out early also prevents ugly cross-hatch marks on the skin!

question: A patient had a deep cut on their shin stitched 8 days ago and asks to remove the stitches. What do you tell them?

options.A: Yes, because leg wounds heal faster than any other body part
options.B: Yes, all sutures can safely come out after exactly seven days
options.C: No, sutures must stay in place for at least a full month
options.D: No, limb and joint wounds usually need ten to fourteen days of healing support

explanation: Areas over joints or shins move a lot and have less blood flow, so they need 10 to 14 days before taking stitches out. Safety first!

question: Which sign tells you right away that a stitched wound might be getting infected?

options.B: Firm skin edges held closely together
options.C: Mild itching around the knot after three days
options.D: A slight pink border immediately after suturing

explanation: Pus (purulent drainage) and skin that feels warm to the touch are classic warning signs that bacteria are multiplying in the wound. Great clinical catch!

question: What is the medical term used when a stitched wound unexpectedly pops open?
explanation: When a wound separates or pops open, we call it dehiscence. It usually happens if there's too much tension or movement before the tissue heals. You're learning pro terminology!
